patients.label: Boy with diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis who presented at three months with a vesiculobullous rash and was treated with off-label omalizumab

identity_evidence.quote: We report an 11‐month‐old boy with diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis

attribution_limitations: The age of 11 months (abstract and table row) is the age at which omalizumab was started; the patient first presented at three months of age. Both ages are recorded under their own attributes.

Source conflict on sequence: the text says the omalizumab dose was escalated to 300 mg and the interval was later shortened to every 3 weeks; the table protocol lists 150 mg every 4 weeks for 6 months, then 150 mg every 3 weeks for 6 months, then 300 mg every 3 weeks. The table regimen fact is quarantined as review_only; the escalation and interval facts carry no order.

The case text states generically that pruritus and flushing start to return if a q21-day omalizumab dose is missed, while the discussion says follow-up demonstrated symptom relapse when a dose was missed. The relapse is recorded as reported by the discussion, but its date, number of occurrences and duration are not stated.
Standard reference doses are given for rupatadine and ketotifen next to the patient's doses; they are general dosing statements, not patient treatment.

Each prednisolone burst is stated to last 4 weeks, while the regimen is 7 days at full dose followed by a taper of 2.5 mg per week until discontinuation; separately, maintenance prednisolone could not be decreased below 7 mg per day. These statements are recorded as printed (arithmetic-only mismatch, not a conflict).
The text calls the stopped drugs systemic corticosteroids; the table cell says oral steroid. The prednisolone route is orally in the regimen sentence, but the stopped item names no route.
Serum tryptase units are printed as μg/L at baseline and as ug/L for the later value and in the discussion.
The rash was initially treated as impetigo; no drug, setting or diagnostic confirmation is stated.
Figure 1 places the post-treatment photograph after 3 months of omalizumab at 14 months of age; the photograph itself adds no stated finding beyond the caption.

claims.text: A three-month-old boy presented with a three-week history of progressively worsening generalized vesiculobullous rash that was initially treated as impetigo. He was otherwise systemically well, with gastroesophageal reflux but no other relevant past medical or family history. Examination showed leathery skin thickening, erythema, vesicles, bullae and erosions with a positive Darier's sign, and no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
